title: How Much Allowance Should I Give My Kid, by Age?
description: Commonly cited allowance ranges by age, per-task vs. fixed weekly pay, and what the research says about docking allowance for missed chores.
h1: How Much Allowance Should I Give My Kid, by Age?
directAnswer: Commonly cited ranges run roughly $0.50 to $1.00 per task for ages 6 to 8, $1.00 to $2.50 for ages 9 to 11, and $2.00 to $5.00 for ages 12 and up, drawn from parenting and chore-chart content rather than a single authority. There's no single correct number for any age. What matters more than the exact dollar figure is consistency: whether it's paid on a predictable schedule and not docked for an occasionally missed chore, which is closer to what the child-development research on motivation actually supports.

sections.heading: Commonly cited allowance ranges by age
sections.html:
AgeCommonly cited range
6–8$0.50–$1.00 per task
9–11$1.00–$2.50 per task
12 and up$2.00–$5.00 per task or a larger weekly amount

These figures are aggregated from multiple parenting and chore-chart sources rather than a single study, and they vary by household income, region, and how many tasks are expected. Treat them as a starting reference point, not a rule.

sections.heading: Per-task vs. a fixed weekly amount
sections.html: Paying per completed task ties the dollar amount directly to effort and is easy for a young child to understand, but it also means allowance fluctuates week to week and can feel like piecework rather than a stable amount to plan around. A fixed weekly allowance, independent of exactly how many chores got done, is simpler to budget on both sides and is the more common structure once a family settles into a routine, with occasional bonuses layered on for extra effort rather than the base amount itself changing.

sections.heading: What the research says about docking pay for a missed chore
sections.html: A body of child-development research generally favors paying a fixed allowance that isn't reduced when a required chore is missed, using non-punitive consequences or separate bonuses instead. The reasoning, drawn from research on intrinsic motivation (Deci, Koestner & Ryan, 1999) and children's helping behaviour (Warneken & Tomasello, 2008), is that docking pay reframes a household contribution as a transaction that can be bought out of, which tends to undermine the habit rather than reinforce it. Other research on family chore practices (Rossmann, 2002; White et al., 2019) informs the broader picture of how chore participation develops over childhood. This is one defensible position, not a universal rule — plenty of families dock allowance for missed chores and it works fine for them.

sections.heading: How the amount should change as a child gets older
sections.html: The jump in these ranges by age band tracks two things at once: kids take on more, and harder, tasks as they get older, and they also want more independent spending money as their social life and interests expand. A common, low-friction pattern is to hold the amount steady between ages rather than adjusting it every few months, then revisit it once — around a birthday, paired with a track record of the current chores being handled consistently — rather than renegotiating on demand.

faq.q: How much allowance should a 6-year-old get?
faq.a: Commonly cited figures run about $0.50 to $1.00 per completed task at this age, though many families use a smaller flat weekly amount instead. There's no fixed correct number; consistency in paying it matters more than the exact figure.

faq.q: How much allowance is normal for a 9 to 11-year-old?
faq.a: Roughly $1.00 to $2.50 per task is a commonly cited range, or an equivalent flat weekly amount in that ballpark. Households vary widely based on income and local cost of living.

faq.q: Should allowance go up automatically with age?
faq.a: Most families increase it gradually as kids take on bigger responsibilities and want more independent spending money, rather than on a fixed schedule. Tying an increase to a birthday plus a track record of consistency is a common, low-friction approach.

faq.q: Should I dock allowance for a missed chore?
faq.a: Research on intrinsic motivation generally favors not docking a fixed allowance for an occasional missed chore, using a separate consequence or bonus system instead, because docking pay can turn a household responsibility into something that feels transactional. It's a defensible stance, not the only correct one — some families do dock pay and it works for them.
